opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. The honest answer is that there are several reasons, and some are practical while others are more personal.

First, the timing. I think we're at a moment where AI can start doing real research: proposing hypotheses, running experiments, analyzing results, and maybe even finding new science. That's what I mean by Auto Research. To pursue it seriously, you need a place where you can build a group quickly, try bold ideas, and not be locked into one narrow direction. In the US, a lot of the frontier energy has moved into big companies, and academia there is under real pressure on funding and compute. At Tsinghua I felt I could build a lab around a long-term vision rather than chasing the next benchmark.

Second, the people. The students here are incredibly strong and hungry. Auto Research isn't only an engineering problem. It sits between AI and the natural sciences, so you need people who are comfortable with math and physics and who also love building systems. Tsinghua has a deep pool of students like that, and many of them are excited about questions that are a bit unconventional.

Third, there's something about the research culture right now in China. There's a lot of momentum, and openness to new paradigms. People are willing to say, "Let's try letting AI do science end to end and see what breaks." That attitude matters when you're working on something where nobody knows the right answer yet.

And on a personal level, I spent many years abroad, at MIT working on things like KANs and the science of deep learning, and I learned a lot there. But I always felt that at some point I wanted to come back and contribute to building the research ecosystem here. Auto Research felt like the right project to do that with. It's ambitious, it's interdisciplinary, and it could really change how science is done. If it works, it shouldn't belong to one country or one company. I hope we can do it in an open way from Tsinghua.

So it wasn't one single reason. It was the combination of the right moment, the right people, and a direction I deeply believe in.

fable-5.1.text:
I'll write the guest response directly.

Honestly, it wasn't an obvious choice to a lot of people around me. I was finishing up at MIT, I'd been working on things like Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks and physics-inspired interpretability, and the default path for someone in my position is to stay in the US, join a big lab or a top department there. So when I said I was going to Tsinghua, people asked why.

For me it came down to what Auto Research actually needs. The vision is AI systems that can run the whole scientific loop themselves: pose a question, design an experiment, run it, read the result, and update their beliefs. That's not a problem you solve with one brilliant paper. It needs a lot of infrastructure, a lot of compute, and a lot of patient, long-horizon building. And it needs people who are willing to work across boundaries, between physics, math, machine learning, and whatever domain you're trying to automate.

Tsinghua has a very unusual density of exactly that kind of talent. The students are extraordinarily strong, and more importantly they're hungry. They haven't been told yet what's impossible. When I talk to undergraduates there about an agent that proposes its own research directions, they don't roll their eyes, they start sketching how to build it. That energy matters enormously for a field that's still being defined.

The second thing is timing and ecosystem. China right now is moving very fast on open models, on agents, on applied AI. There's a sense that the next few years are the window where the foundations of this field get laid, and I wanted to be somewhere that felt like the center of motion rather than the center of established consensus. Being early in a place that's accelerating is worth more to me than being comfortable in a place that's already peaked on this particular question.

And there's a personal dimension too. I grew up in China, I did my undergraduate work at Peking University, and I always felt I'd want to bring back what I learned abroad. Science is global, but institutions are local, and if I believe Auto Research is going to reshape how science is done, I'd like to help build that capacity at home, not just contribute to it from a distance.

So I'd put it this way: I didn't see it as choosing between east and west. I saw it as choosing the place where I thought the thing I care most about could actually get built, with the people I thought could build it.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, the key question was where I could best pursue the research I really wanted to do: using AI to help automate scientific discovery. That takes more than building a model. It takes close interaction with people who understand the scientific problems and can tell you whether the results are meaningful.

I saw Tsinghua as a place where I could bring those pieces together and have room to explore a longer-term direction. So the attraction was the opportunity to build an environment around that research vision, with students and collaborators who wanted to pursue it together.
